title: Dating the Kings
lead: Kings dates each ruler of Israel and Judah by the other kingdom's reign and gives the length of each reign, but the figures do not always agree. Scholars have built several systems, anchored by Assyrian and Egyptian records, to turn them into dates BC.

sections.h: The problem and the main solutions
sections.b: A typical entry gives the year of the other kingdom's king, the new king's age (for Judah), the length of reign and the queen mother (1 Kings 15:1–2, 9–10, 25, 33). Added up, the two lines drift apart, and some synchronisms contradict the lengths (2 Kings 8:16; 2 Kings 15:30, 33). Edwin Thiele explained most differences by co-regencies, two ways of counting a king's first year, and different new-year months, dating the split to 931/930 BC. Gershon Galil's revised system gives the same date, and K. A. Kitchen gives 931. Hayim Tadmor, followed by Mordechai Cogan, puts it about 928. John Hayes and Paul Hooker reject co-regencies and allow for scribal errors, which gives about 927/926. W. F. Albright's older and independent system (1945) gave 922. Many critics think the numbers came from different sources and include errors. The Greek translation sometimes has different figures: it lacks the Asa dates at 1 Kings 16:8 and 16:15, dates Jehoshaphat's accession to Omri's eleventh year (16:28a) and Ahab's to Jehoshaphat's second year (16:29). Outside anchors include Shishak's raid (about 925 BC), Ahab at Qarqar (853 BC), Jehu's tribute (841 BC) and the fall of Samaria (722 BC).

The final four reigns matter to Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel and 2 Kings 22–25. The dates below are the usual ones, with the records that fix them. Josiah, 640–609 BC, was killed at Megiddo by Neco in 609 (2 Kings 23:29–30); the Babylonian Chronicle shows Egypt marching to help Assyria at Harran that year. Jehoiakim, 609–598, ruled through the battle of Carchemish in 605 and died in December 598. Jehoiachin reigned three months, 598–597; Jerusalem surrendered on 16 March 597 according to the Babylonian Chronicle, and ration tablets from Babylon name Ya'ukin, king of Judah. Zedekiah, 597–586, was the last king; Jerusalem fell in the fifth month (Av) of 586, which some scholars date to 587. Jeremiah's call is dated to Josiah's thirteenth year, 627 BC (Jeremiah 1:2).
